---
title: "Quiz: region properties and moments"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Coordinates: $x$ = column, $y$ = row (down); orientations are counter-clockwise as seen on the screen.

---

**Q1.** Why can area, centroid and second moments of all objects be computed in a single scan of the label image?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What kind of quantity is each of them?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
They are sums over the pixels of an object ($\sum 1$, $\sum x$, $\sum y$, $\sum x^2$, $\sum xy$, $\sum y^2$). Keep one set of running sums per label and add each pixel to the sums of its label. Central moments follow from the raw sums afterwards.
:::

---

**Q2.** You measure the perimeter of digitised discs by counting pixel edges, at higher and higher resolution. Does the estimate converge to $2\pi r$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How long is a staircase compared with the straight line it follows?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. A staircase is as long as its horizontal plus vertical legs, however fine its steps. Averaged over all directions of a circle this is $4/\pi \approx 1.27$ times the true length: the edge count tends to $8r$, not $2\pi r$.
:::

---

**Q3.** What do the eigenvectors and eigenvalues of the second-moment matrix $S$ of an object tell you?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Treat the pixels as a cloud of points (the PCA unit).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The eigenvectors are the principal axes of the pixel cloud: $\mathbf v_1$ points along the direction in which the object is longest (its orientation), $\mathbf v_2$ across it. The eigenvalues are the variances of the pixel coordinates along these axes; the equivalent ellipse has semi-axes $2\sqrt{\lambda_1}$ and $2\sqrt{\lambda_2}$.
:::

---

**Q4.** An object is rotated by 30°. Which of these change: $S$, $\lambda_1$, $\lambda_2$, the orientation, the eccentricity?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$S = Q\Lambda Q^\top$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$S$ and the orientation change (the orientation by 30°). $\lambda_1$, $\lambda_2$ and the eccentricity do not: rotation turns the eigenvectors and keeps the eigenvalues (up to small digitisation changes).
:::

---

**Q5.** A program reports the orientation of a square as 0°, and of the same square rotated by 20° also as 0°. Is it broken?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compare the two eigenvalues of a square.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. A square has $\lambda_1 = \lambda_2$, like a disc: every direction is a principal axis, and the second moments cannot see any orientation. The reported angle is arbitrary and should not be used.
:::

---

**Q6.** An L-shaped object and a solid ellipse have the same equivalent ellipse. What does that say about the equivalent ellipse?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How many numbers define it?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The ellipse is fixed by six numbers (area, centroid, the three entries of $S$). Many different shapes share them: it summarises the spread of the pixels, not the outline. Shape features beyond moments (next unit) tell the L and the ellipse apart.
:::

---

**Q7.** What is the Euler number of: a ring; the digit 8; two separate discs; a disc with three holes?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Objects minus holes.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Ring: $1 - 1 = 0$. Digit 8: $1 - 2 = -1$. Two discs: $2 - 0 = 2$. Disc with three holes: $1 - 3 = -2$.
:::

---

**Q8.** Why is it surprising that the Euler number can be computed from $2 \times 2$ windows alone?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Counting objects or holes seems to need global information.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Whether two far-apart pixels belong to the same object is a global question, so counting objects or holes separately needs labelling. Their **difference** is a topological invariant that is a sum of local contributions (Euler's formula $V - E + F$), so a single scan over $2 \times 2$ windows suffices.
:::

---

**Q9.** *(math)* Show that $\mu_{20} = m_{20} - m_{10}^2/m_{00}$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Expand $(x - \bar x)^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\mu_{20} = \sum (x^2 - 2x\bar x + \bar x^2) = m_{20} - 2\bar x m_{10} + \bar x^2 m_{00}$. With $\bar x = m_{10}/m_{00}$: $m_{20} - 2m_{10}^2/m_{00} + m_{10}^2/m_{00} = m_{20} - m_{10}^2/m_{00}$.
:::
